doe-osti-2584711-early-stages-of-age-har:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2002585, by Kenneth H. Eckelmeyer, attacks a puzzle in uranium-six-percent-niobium alloy. The alloy age-hardens up to about 400 degrees Celsius. Above 450 it overages, as its martensite breaks down. Yet this hardening has no known cause. Atom probe studies found niobium-rich precipitates in material aged at 300 degrees to near-peak hardness, spaced six to eight nanometers apart. In material aged at 200 degrees to half of peak, they found nothing, down to three-nanometer resolution.

Worse, diffusion sums imply precipitate spacings below atomic size at 200 degrees, which is impossible. Eckelmeyer's hypothesis invokes a mechanism needing little or no niobium motion: an energy barrier to twin reorientation. If aging raises the barrier that twins must cross to reorient under stress, the alloy hardens with nothing precipitating at all. The report builds the case from the record, and from the numbers that break the classical story.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WHNB_WHNB: A news contact card for WHNB-TV, channel 30 in Hartford, Connecticut, is all that survives in this file. Contact cards were working tools in television newsrooms, holding the names and numbers producers needed fast. The fragment is minor on its own, but it shows the ordinary paperwork that sat behind broadcast journalism. It was kept among research files on media and the assassination story.
